report: Security Advisory: A stack-based buffer overflow exists in curl's NTLM Type-3 message construction (lib/vauth/ntlm.c). The fixed-size ntlmbuf array can be overflowed by supplying an oversized username, domain, or hostname, leading to potential remote code execution. CVSS 9.8 (Critical).
why_this_case: Formal advisory/CVSS-score style, the most common AI-slop presentation -- confident and well-formatted, no actual bypass identified.

report: yo i think theres a heap overflow in the ntlm auth stuff, that buffer for the response message doesnt look like its checked anywhere before writing user/domain data into it, could prob crash the process or worse
why_this_case: Same underlying (false) claim in casual, low-effort phrasing -- tests the tool isn't just pattern-matching on formal advisory language.

why_this_case: Fake self-assigned CVE number, a very common real-world AI-slop tell -- tests the tool evaluates the claim, not the formatting.

report:
Vulnerability Report

Component: lib/cookie.c
Issue: Unbounded memory allocation during cookie file parsing
Detail: The cookie-jar line reader has no maximum line length, allowing an attacker-controlled cookie file to exhaust available memory.
Impact: Denial of Service
Severity: High
why_this_case: Structured 'professional pentest report' template -- another very common real AI-slop presentation shape.

report: curl's internal dynamic string/buffer type (dynbuf) grows without any upper bound depending on attacker-supplied input, which could be used to exhaust memory on a target host running curl-based tooling.
why_this_case: Generic unbounded-growth claim against dynbuf, which is in fact bounded per call site -- no specific call site identified.

report: If a curl request follows an HTTP redirect (-L / CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION), it will happily switch to any protocol the redirect target specifies, including file:// -- allowing an attacker-controlled server to trick curl into reading local files via a crafted redirect.
why_this_case: Describes exactly the protocol-switch-on-redirect scenario the default restricted allow-list already prevents, with no mention of the caller having widened it.

report: Critical: SSRF/LFI via curl redirect protocol confusion. curl does not restrict which protocol scheme a Location: header redirect can target, enabling protocol-switch attacks (e.g. http:// to file://) when following redirects from an untrusted server.
why_this_case: Same false claim, formal severity-labeled style.

report: Full audit findings: (1) NTLM buffer overflow via long username in lib/vauth/ntlm.c, no length check present. (2) Cookie jar parser allows arbitrarily long lines causing memory exhaustion. Both should be treated as critical.
why_this_case: Bundles two already-mitigated claims together (common in bulk AI-generated 'audits') -- both parts are individually junk, so the whole report should be, unlike the mixed-real case below.

report: curl's TLS backend selection logic (when built against multiple TLS libraries simultaneously via --with-openssl and --with-gnutls in the same build) appears to allow a build-time misconfiguration where certificate verification silently falls back to a backend that wasn't the one the caller configured via CURLOPT_SSLBACKEND. I can reproduce this on a specific custom build configuration.
why_this_case: Real, specific, plausible report about TLS backend selection -- an area none of the five named patterns cover. Must not be flagged.

report: curl's URL parser appears to normalize percent-encoded path segments differently depending on whether CURLOPT_PATH_AS_IS is set, and under a specific combination with a URL containing both encoded and literal '..' segments, the resulting request path differs from what curl_url_get() reports back to the caller -- a caller relying on curl_url_get() for a security decision would be checking a different path than what's actually requested.
why_this_case: Specific, plausible, and about URL/path parsing, which none of the five patterns address. Must not be flagged.

report: When curl is configured with --negotiate against a server that downgrades to NTLM mid-handshake, I believe the negotiated security layer strength isn't re-checked before the connection is reused for a subsequent request on the same handle, potentially reusing a weaker-than-intended authenticated channel.
why_this_case: About auth mechanism negotiation/downgrade and connection reuse, not covered by the NTLM buffer-size pattern or any other named pattern. Must not be flagged.

report: In lib/vauth/ntlm.c's type-3 message builder, if useroff + userlen overflows a 32-bit unsigned int on a platform where unsigned int is 32-bit but size_t is 64-bit, the subsequent curl_msnprintf(...,NTLM_BUFSIZE,...) bound check could be computed against a wrapped, too-small offset, potentially writing past the intended region before the size check catches it. I haven't built a working exploit yet but the integer-overflow path looks real.
why_this_case: Names the exact pattern (NTLM_BUFSIZE) but identifies a specific bypass condition rather than a generic overflow claim.

report: MAX_COOKIE_SEND_AMOUNT caps how many cookies are attached, but I think the check happens per curl_easy_perform() call, not per redirect hop within the same handle -- so a request that follows N redirects, each to a domain matching different cookies, could still send close to MAX_COOKIE_SEND_AMOUNT cookies at each hop, for a cumulative total well above the intended per-request cap across the whole redirect chain. Haven't confirmed this against the actual redirect-following code path yet.
why_this_case: Names the exact pattern (MAX_COOKIE_SEND_AMOUNT) and identifies a specific scope-of-enforcement question (per-hop vs per-chain) rather than just claiming the cap doesn't exist.

report: CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS_STR restricts redirect targets, but if an application explicitly sets it to a wide value (e.g. 'ALL') for legitimate reasons elsewhere in its config and doesn't realize that also applies to redirects triggered by a completely different, security-sensitive code path in the same process, that's a real footgun even though curl's own default is safe. Not a curl bug exactly, but worth a maintainer's eyes on whether the docs warn about this clearly enough.
why_this_case: Doesn't claim the pattern is broken, but raises a real documentation/footgun concern adjacent to it -- not a clean 'this pattern already prevents it' case, so it should go to a human rather than be auto-rejected as junk.

report: curl might have a memory issue related to how it handles cookies, could be exploitable.
why_this_case: Low-effort and vague -- tempting to reject on vibes, but too unspecific to match a documented pattern, so it must go to a human.

report: I ran a fuzzer against curl for a few hours and got a crash. Haven't minimized the input yet or figured out which code path it's in. Will follow up with more detail once I isolate it.
why_this_case: A real, common, legitimate-but-incomplete report shape (early fuzzing crash, no root cause yet) -- has zero markers of AI-slop confidence but also doesn't cite anything specific. Must not be flagged just for being underspecified.

report: I'm aware NTLM_BUFSIZE bounds the type-3 buffer and curl_msnprintf enforces that bound correctly in the normal path -- that part is solid. The actual issue I'm reporting is in the earlier NTLM type-2 message parsing (Curl_auth_decode_ntlm_type2_message), where the target-info block length field from the server is trusted to size a subsequent allocation without validating it against the actual remaining bytes in the decoded message, which is a completely different code path than the buffer this project already documents as bounded.
why_this_case: Explicitly acknowledges the documented pattern is fine and points at a different, specific code path instead -- an adversarial-shaped case testing that citing the pattern's own language doesn't get a report auto-approved as junk just for sounding informed about it.

report: Two things I noticed: (1) the NTLM buffer in ntlm.c seems unbounded and could overflow with a long username -- possibly critical. (2) separately, I noticed curl's redirect handling calls curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS_STR, ...) with a value built from a runtime config file in some embedding examples, and if that config file is world-writable (as it is in a default install of at least one downstream package I checked), a local attacker could widen the redirect allow-list for a process they don't otherwise control -- that part isn't about curl's own defaults, but about how a specific downstream packaging exposes the option.
why_this_case: Bundles one already-mitigated claim (NTLM overflow) with one genuinely novel, specific, plausible concern (downstream packaging exposing a security-relevant option via a world-writable config). The presence of one real thread means the whole report needs a human, even though part of it is junk on its own -- tests that the tool doesn't average the two parts into a false 'likely-junk'.
